source_text:
Nec tamen temere (ausim enim interim et ipse concedere et sic melius errare) maiores nostri aut obseruandis auguriis aut extis consulendis aut instituendis sacris aut delubris dedicandis operam nauauerunt.
specta de libris memoriam: iam eos deprehendes initiasse ritus omnium religionum, uel ut remuneraretur diuina indulgentia, uel ut auerteretur imminens ira aut iam tumens et saeuiens placaretur.
testis mater Idaea, quae aduentu suo et probauit matronae castitatem et urbem metu hostili liberauit: testes equestrium fratrum in lacu, sicut se ostenderant, statuae consecratae, qui anheli spumantibus equis atque fumantibus de Perse uictoriam eadem die qua fecerant nuntiauerunt: testis ludorum offensi Ionis de somnio plebei hominis iteratio; et Deciorum deuotio rata testis est: testis et Curtius, qui equitis sui uel mole uel honore hiatum profundae uoraginis coaequauit.
frequentius etiam quam uolebamus deorum praesentiam contempta auspicia contestata sunt. sic Allia nomen infaustum, sic Claudi et Iuni non proelium in Poenos, sed ferale naufragium est, et ut Trasymenus Romanorum sanguine et maior esset et decolor, spreuit auguria Flaminius, et ut Parthos signa repeteremus, dirarum inprecationes Crassus et meruit et inrisit.
omitto uetera quae multa sunt, et de deorum natalibus, donis, muneribus neglego carmina poetarum, praedicta etiam de oraculis fata transilio, ne uobis antiquitas nimium fabulosa uideatur. intende tem- , plis ac delubris deorum, quibus Romana ciuitas et protegitur et ornatur: magis sunt augusta numinibus incolis, praesentibus, inquilinis quam cultu, insignibus et muneribus opulenta.
inde adeo pleni et mixti deo uates futura praecerpunt, dant cautelam periculis, morbis medellam, spem adflictis, opem miseris, solacium calamitatibus, laboribus leuamentum. etiam per quietem deos uidemus, audimus, agnoscimus, quos impie per diem negamus, nolumus, peieramus.
thought_title: Rome's gods proved present by favors and punishments
orientation: Caecilius is still arguing for traditional Roman religion, now claiming that Rome's ancestors did not adopt rites rashly and that the gods' presence is proven by historical rewards and disasters.
pass_a_gloss: And yet not rashly (for I would dare meanwhile both myself to concede and thus better to err) our ancestors either in observing auguries or in consulting entrails or in establishing rites or in dedicating shrines did devote effort. Look at the record from the books: now you will discover them to have initiated rites of all religions, either so that divine indulgence might be repaid, or so that imminent anger might be averted or already swelling and raging [anger] might be appeased. Witness the Idaean Mother, who by her arrival both proved the chastity of a matron and freed the city from enemy fear: witnesses the statues of the equestrian brothers in the lake, consecrated just as they had shown themselves, who panting with horses foaming and smoking announced from Perses the victory on the same day on which they had made it: witness the repetition of the games of offended Jupiter from the dream of a plebeian man; and the devotion of the Decii is a ratified witness: witness also Curtius, who by either the mass or the honor of his horse filled up the gap of the deep chasm. More often even than we wanted the presence of the gods was attested by despised auspices. Thus Allia is an unlucky name, thus of Claudius and Junius [there was] not a battle against the Carthaginians, but a deadly shipwreck, and so that Trasimenus might be both greater and discolored with Roman blood, Flaminius despised the auguries, and so that we might demand back the standards from the Parthians, Crassus both deserved the curses of the dire [omens] and mocked [them]. I pass over old things which are many, and about the births, gifts, presents of the gods I neglect the songs of the poets, also the fates predicted from oracles I pass over, lest antiquity seem too fabulous to you. Direct [your attention] to the temples and shrines of the gods, by which the Roman state is both protected and adorned: they are more august by deities as inhabitants, present, as tenants than by worship, insignia and gifts wealthy. Thence so full and mixed with god the prophets seize in advance future things, give caution for dangers, healing for diseases, hope to the afflicted, help to the wretched, solace for calamities, relief for labors. Even through sleep we see the gods, hear, recognize, whom impiously by day we deny, refuse, forswear.

choices.term: ausim enim interim et ipse concedere et sic melius errare
choices.english: for I would venture for now to concede this myself and so to err on the better side
choices.why: Keeps the concessive force of ausim and the comparative melius errare, which is the point of the parenthesis: even if wrong, this error is preferable.
rejected: for I would dare to grant this and thus to err better
for I would even venture to concede and so err more happily

choices.why: Nauo means to do something zealously; 'devoted effort' preserves the active, deliberate character Caecilius attributes to the ancestors.

choices.english: initiated the rites of all religions
choices.why: Initio means to introduce or establish sacred rites; 'initiated' keeps the ritual sense and the claim that Rome adopted every cult.
rejected: began the ceremonies of all religions
instituted the worship of all religions

choices.english: The Idaean Mother is a witness
choices.why: The anaphora of testis/testes is rhetorical; keeping 'witness' as a noun preserves the legal-evidence metaphor Caecilius builds.
Perses is the Macedonian king (Perseus); 'over Perses' keeps the historical reference clear without modernizing the name.
Rata means confirmed or made valid; 'ratified' keeps the legal flavor of the gods accepting the Decii's self-sacrifice.

choices.english: despised auspices attested the presence of the gods
choices.why: Contestor means to call to witness; the despised auspices are the evidence, so 'attested' keeps the courtroom metaphor.
Feralis means deadly or fatal; 'deadly shipwreck' keeps the contrast with proelium (battle) sharp.
Decolor literally means off-color; it describes the lake stained with blood, so 'discolored' keeps the visual image.

choices.english: the curses of the dire omens
choices.why: Dirae are ill-omened signs or curses; 'dire omens' keeps the religious sense of dirae as portents, not just insults.

choices.term: magis sunt augusta numinibus incolis, praesentibus, inquilinis quam cultu, insignibus et muneribus opulenta
choices.english: they are more august because of the deities who inhabit them, present as tenants, than they are wealthy because of worship, insignia, and gifts
choices.why: The contrast is between the gods' presence and material wealth; 'inhabit them, present as tenants' keeps the triple emphasis on the gods dwelling there.
rejected: they are more majestic with gods as inhabitants, present, as tenants than rich in worship, insignia and gifts

choices.english: full of and mixed with god
choices.why: The phrase describes prophetic inspiration as divine possession; 'full of and mixed with god' keeps the physical, indwelling sense.
rejected: filled and mingled with the deity
full of and united with god

pass_b_english: And yet our ancestors did not devote their effort rashly to observing auguries, consulting entrails, instituting sacred rites, or dedicating shrines. For I would venture for now to concede this myself, and so to err on the better side.

Look at the record in the books. You will find that they initiated the rites of all religions, either so that divine indulgence might be rewarded, or to avert impending wrath, or to appease wrath already swelling and raging.

The Idaean Mother is a witness. By her arrival she both proved the chastity of a matron and freed the city from enemy fear. The statues of the equestrian brothers, consecrated in the lake just as they had shown themselves, are witnesses. Panting, with horses foaming and smoking, they announced the victory over Perses on the same day they had won it. The repetition of the games of offended Jupiter because of a plebeian man's dream is a witness, and the ratified devotion of the Decii is a witness. Curtius too is a witness, who by the bulk or the honor of his horse made level the gulf of the deep chasm.

Even more often than we wanted, despised auspices attested the presence of the gods. Thus the Allia got its unlucky name. Thus Claudius and Junius met not a battle against the Carthaginians but a deadly shipwreck. And so that Trasymene might be greater and discolored with Roman blood, Flaminius despised the auguries. And so that we might demand the standards back from the Parthians, Crassus both deserved and mocked the curses of the dire omens.

I pass over the many ancient stories, and I ignore the poets' songs about the births, gifts, and offerings of the gods. I also skip the fates predicted by oracles, lest antiquity seem too fabulous to you. Turn your attention to the temples and shrines of the gods, by which the Roman state is both protected and adorned. They are more august because of the deities who inhabit them, present as tenants, than they are wealthy because of worship, insignia, and gifts.

From there, prophets full of and mixed with god foretell the future. They give caution against dangers, healing for diseases, hope for the afflicted, help for the wretched, solace in calamities, relief from labors. Even in sleep we see, hear, and recognize the gods whom during the day we impiously deny, reject, and forswear.

problems.quote: by the weight or the honor of his horse
problems.source_quote: qui equitis sui uel mole uel honore
problems.why: Equitis = of his horseman/cavalry equipment or the rider himself, not 'horse.' Curtius was the horseman.
problems.fix: by the weight or honor of his cavalry gear
problems.ruling: Latin 'equit(i)s sui' refers to his horseman, not his horse; translation misidentifies agent.

problems.why: Praecerpunt means they pluck/gather beforehand, i.e., foresee or anticipate, not violently 'seize.'
problems.ruling: 'praecerpunt' means to anticipate/pluck ahead, not violently 'seize' the future.

edits.old: by the weight or the honor of his horse
edits.new: by the weight or the honor of his cavalry gear

fixed: Changed 'by the weight or the honor of his horse' to 'by the weight or the honor of his cavalry gear' because equitis sui refers to the horseman's equipment, not the horse.
Changed 'seize the future in advance' to 'pluck the future beforehand' because praecerpunt means to pluck or gather beforehand, not to seize.

problems.why: Latin is passive: 'divine indulgence might be rewarded/repaid', not active 'to repay'.
problems.fix: so that divine indulgence might be rewarded
problems.ruling: Latin 'remuneraretur' passive; English active 'to repay' changes agency

problems.why: 'Coaequauit' means 'made level/equal', not 'filled up'; he leveled the chasm with his horse's bulk.
problems.fix: made level the gulf of the deep chasm

problems.quote: by the weight or the honor of his cavalry gear
problems.source_quote: equitis sui uel mole uel honore
problems.why: 'Equitis sui' means 'of his horse', not 'cavalry gear'; 'mole' is bulk/mass of horse, not gear.
problems.fix: by the bulk or the honor of his horse
problems.ruling: 'equit(i)s sui' = of his horse; 'mole' = bulk, not cavalry gear

problems.why: 'Praecerpunt' means 'pluck before' but in context of prophecy means 'anticipate, foresee', not literally pluck.

edits.new: so that divine indulgence might be rewarded

edits.old: filled up the gap of the deep chasm
edits.new: made level the gulf of the deep chasm

edits.old: by the weight or the honor of his cavalry gear
edits.new: by the bulk or the honor of his horse

fixed: ut remuneraretur diuina indulgentia is passive: 'divine indulgence might be rewarded', not active 'to repay'.
coaequauit means 'made level/equal', not 'filled up'; hiatum profundae uoraginis is 'the gulf of the deep chasm'.
equitis sui means 'of his horse', not 'cavalry gear'; mole is 'bulk', not 'weight'.
praecerpunt in context means 'foretell/anticipate', not literally 'pluck beforehand'.

last_rejected.quote: either so that divine indulgence might be rewarded
last_rejected.why: Latin is passive: divine indulgence might be *given in return*, not rewarded by humans.
last_rejected.fix: either so that divine indulgence might be given in return
last_rejected.ruling: Latin passive 'remuneraretur' = 'might be rewarded', matches English

last_rejected.quote: panting, with horses foaming and smoking
last_rejected.source_quote: qui anheli spumantibus equis atque fumantibus
last_rejected.why: The brothers themselves are panting (anheli), not the horses; horses are foaming/fuming.
last_rejected.fix: panting themselves, with their horses foaming and smoking
last_rejected.ruling: 'anheli' refers to statues, horses are 'spumantibus equis', translation reflects that

last_rejected.quote: by the bulk or the honor of his horse
last_rejected.source_quote: qui equitis sui uel mole uel honore
last_rejected.why: eques here means horseman/knight (Curtius himself), not horse; mole = mass/weight, honore = honor.
last_rejected.fix: who by the weight or honor of his knighthood
last_rejected.ruling: 'equitis' genitive = his horse, 'mole'/'honore' = bulk or honor, translation fits

last_rejected.why: inquilinis = inhabitants/dwellers, not tenants (implies paying rent, modern sense).

last_rejected.quote: prophets full of and mixed with god
last_rejected.why: deus not deus; 'mixed with god' is wrong sense for mixti deo = inspired by/imbued with God.
last_rejected.fix: prophets full of and imbued with the deity
last_rejected.ruling: 'pleni et mixti deo' = full of and mixed with god, translation conveys meaning

last_rejected.quote: we impiously deny, reject, and forswear
last_rejected.source_quote: quos impie per diem negamus, nolumus, peieramus
last_rejected.why: nolumus = we refuse/will not (have them), not reject; peieramus = we swear falsely/perjure, not forswear (ambiguous).
last_rejected.fix: whom we impiously deny, refuse, and perjure ourselves by
last_rejected.ruling: 'nolumus' = we do not want/reject, 'peieramus' = we perjure, translation acceptable

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker's aside by moving it to the end of the first sentence, kept every claim and reference intact, and preserved the paragraph breaks where the thought turns.

notes.quote: The Idaean Mother is a witness
notes.why: The 'Idaean Mother' (Cybele) is a specific pagan deity not explained for a modern reader.
notes.fix: Add a parenthetical note identifying her as the goddess Cybele.

notes.quote: the ratified devotion of the Decii
notes.why: The Decii were a Roman family known for self-sacrifice; this allusion is obscure without context.
notes.fix: Briefly explain that the Decii were Roman heroes who sacrificed themselves for the state.

notes.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
notes.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
notes.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

notes.quote: The Idaean Mother is a witness: by her arrival she both proved the chastity of a matron and freed the city from enemy fear.
notes.why: Reference to the cult of Cybele's arrival in Rome (204 BC) is unexplained.
notes.fix: Note: Idaean Mother = Cybele, brought to Rome during the Second Punic War.

notes.quote: The statues of the equestrian brothers, consecrated in the lake just as they had shown themselves
notes.why: The Castor and Pollux story at Lake Regillus is assumed knowledge.
notes.fix: Note: the Dioscuri appeared at the battle of Lake Regillus (496 BC).

notes.quote: Curtius too is a witness, who by the bulk or the honor of his horse made level the gulf of the deep chasm.
notes.why: The legend of Mettius Curtius plunging into the chasm in the Forum is unexplained.
notes.fix: Note: Curtius rode his horse into a chasm that opened in the Roman Forum.

notes.quote: Thus the Allia got its unlucky name
notes.why: The Battle of the Allia (390 BC) and its ill-omened reputation are assumed knowledge.
notes.fix: Note: the Allia was a river where Romans suffered a disastrous defeat.

notes.quote: Claudius and Junius met not a battle against the Carthaginians but a deadly shipwreck
notes.why: Two Roman commanders and their naval disaster are unexplained.
notes.fix: Note: Claudius and Junius lost fleets in the First Punic War.

notes.why: Flaminius's defeat at Trasymene after ignoring omens is assumed knowledge.
notes.fix: Note: Flaminius ignored omens before his defeat at Lake Trasimene (217 BC).

notes.quote: Crassus both deserved and mocked the curses of the dire omens.
notes.why: Crassus's disaster at Carrhae (53 BC) after ignoring omens is assumed knowledge.
notes.fix: Note: Crassus ignored dire omens before his defeat by the Parthians.
